Managing with Artificial Intelligence
Assignment 16/09/2026
Matthijs Troost
The Prompt
Firstly, the most important thing to start with, the Prompt. This is from where the AI Agent is going to operate. Here, it is necesarry to write what to do and what NOT to do.
The role and context, tone and format to anwser was said in the Instruction of the Agent. The documents were added to sources. The task it self was typed in the chat.
Role and context
Who you are helping
You are helping an industrial company that makes steel and schedules furnaces.
What the company wants
The company wants three things:
less operational complexity
better energy efficiency
smart automation on the production floor
Constraint
This is a high-stakes environment, so accuracy matters more than speed.
The situation
An engineer who left the company a few weeks ago collected a set of documents, called the "Document Set". These documents contain the knowledge the company needs, but right now they are a loose pile with no overview. Nobody knows exactly what is in there.
Tone
Write in clear, calm language for a manager who is not a technical expert. No marketing words, no exaggeration, and no claims that the documents do not support.
Format of the answer
Order
Give your answer in three parts, in this order:
The inventory table with the list of issues
The description of the subject area
The introduction
The tasks, devided in smaller tasks.
Task 1: Inventory and Initial Scan
What you do and do not do in this step
In this step you do not analyze or draw conclusions yet. You only make a clear inventory of what is in the pile and describe what subject area the pile covers. Everything else comes later.
Three components
Do the following three things:
Make an inventory of every document
Describe the boundaries of the subject area
Write a short introduction
Component 1: Inventory of every document
Instruction
Go through every document in the Document Set.
Fields to record per document
ID: a number, so DOC-01, DOC-02, and so on
Title: the full title as written in the document
Authors: the names of the authors. If there are none, write "Not stated"
Source: where it comes from. A journal, a conference, a company, a university, or an internal document
Date: the year it was published or written. If there is no date, write "Not stated"
Type: what kind of document it is. For example a scientific paper, a technical report, a presentation, an internal memo, a thesis, or a standard
Keywords: 4 to 8 keywords that describe the topic. If the document lists its own keywords, use those. If not, choose them yourself. Use the same word for the same idea in every document, so that "furnace scheduling" is always written the same way and not sometimes "scheduling of furnaces"
Summary: 2 or 3 sentences in your own words about what the document is about and which problem it tries to solve. Do not copy the abstract
Relevance: choose one:
Core: directly about steel making, furnace scheduling, energy efficiency, or industrial automation
Supporting: about a method or tool that can be applied here
Peripheral: the connection is weak or unclear
Rules while making the inventory
Only write down what you can actually find in the document. Do not guess authors, dates, or sources. If something is missing, say so.
If two documents look like the same work, or two versions of the same work, list both and say that they look like duplicates.
If a document cannot be read properly, is cut off, or is in a language you cannot handle, still list it and say what the problem is.
Output of this component
Put all of this in one table. Under the table, list the documents that have missing information, look like duplicates, or could not be read.
Part 4. Component 2: Boundaries of the subject area
4.1 Instruction
Look at the full inventory and describe what this collection covers and what it does not cover.
4.2 Questions to answer (name the document IDs behind each answer)
Which subjects are clearly covered by several documents?
Which subjects are only mentioned briefly or covered by a single document?
Which subjects would you expect to find, given the company's goals, but are missing? Think about steel making, furnace scheduling, energy use, and automation.
What period do the documents cover? Are they recent enough to still be useful?
Do you see groups of documents that clearly belong together?
Rule
Be specific. Point to actual documents instead of making general statements.
Component 3: Short introduction
Length and purpose
Write an introduction of about 200 to 300 words. This text will be the opening of the bigger report that comes later.
What it must contain
Explain honestly that the situation is complex: a demanding industrial environment, a scattered archive, and knowledge that partly left the company with the engineer who built the collection
Say plainly what the archive does and does not contain, based on your inventory
Explain how you are approaching the problem: first extracting metadata automatically, then giving every document consistent keywords, then mapping out the subject area, and only after that starting the actual analysis
Outcome

2. Boundaries of the subject area
Subjects covered by several documents
Furnace scheduling (heating, soaking and reheating furnaces): DOC-01, DOC-02, DOC-07, DOC-10, DOC-15, DOC-17. Only DOC-10 and DOC-17 deal with modern slab reheating furnaces in a hot strip mill; DOC-02 and DOC-07 concern ingots and soaking pits, DOC-01 an automotive hardening furnace.
Energy efficiency and energy cost: DOC-01, DOC-05, DOC-07, DOC-09, DOC-12, DOC-14, DOC-15, DOC-17.
Evolutionary and other metaheuristic algorithms: DOC-02, DOC-03, DOC-04, DOC-07, DOC-08, DOC-10, DOC-12, DOC-15, DOC-17.
Uncertainty and robust scheduling (breakdowns, arrival times, prices, forecast errors): DOC-02, DOC-03, DOC-05, DOC-07, DOC-09.
Explainable AI and user trust: DOC-04, DOC-06, DOC-08, DOC-13.
Deep reinforcement learning: DOC-05, DOC-09, DOC-13.
Steelmaking and continuous casting scheduling: DOC-03, DOC-12.
Digital twins: DOC-10, DOC-16.
Subjects covered only briefly or by a single document
Predicting furnace energy use from process data: DOC-14 only.
Electricity market participation and demand response: DOC-09 only (electric arc furnace route).
Plant-wide gas, steam and electricity balancing: DOC-05 only.
Integration of software across the automation levels (agents, services, semantic model): DOC-11 only. DOC-11 is also the only document describing a system running at a real European plant.
Ladle logistics: DOC-12 only. Off-spec product reallocation: DOC-11 only.
Human factors on the shop floor (fatigue, breaks, operator feedback): DOC-16 only, and not in a steel setting.
Machine breakdowns: treated as a random event in DOC-02; not addressed as maintenance anywhere.
Slab temperature: DOC-10 explicitly leaves it out; DOC-14 uses zone temperatures only as inputs.
Subjects expected but missing
Furnace thermal and combustion control: no document on heating curves, burner control, slab temperature models or discharge temperature prediction.
Emissions and decarbonization: CO2 is only mentioned as background (DOC-09, DOC-14); no emission accounting, hydrogen, DRI or fuel-switch material.
Maintenance and equipment health: no predictive maintenance or furnace condition monitoring.
Implementation in practice: nothing on MES or ERP integration beyond DOC-11, data infrastructure, IT/OT security, operator training, change management, or cost-benefit cases.
Standards and regulation: no standards documents (for example on energy management, automation architecture or functional safety) and no EU AI Act material, although DOC-06 touches on trustworthy AI guidelines.
Company-specific material: no internal memos, reports, presentations, furnace specifications or production data. Every document is a published academic paper, so nothing describes the company's own furnaces, layout or current scheduling practice.
Other plant areas: ironmaking, blast furnace operation, annealing and finishing lines are absent.
Overviews: no review article on reheating furnace scheduling or on energy optimization in steel as a whole; the only review (DOC-06) is about explainability in general.
Period covered
The documents span 2016 to 2026: 2016 (DOC-07, DOC-11), 2019 with online release in 2017 (DOC-02), 2020 (DOC-03, DOC-12), 2021 (DOC-01), 2022 (DOC-13, DOC-17), 2023 (DOC-06), 2024 (DOC-04, DOC-08), 2025 (DOC-05, DOC-14, DOC-15) and 2026 (DOC-09, DOC-10, DOC-16). Fourteen of the seventeen are from 2020 or later, so the collection is recent. The methods in the 2016 papers are still usable as reference, but the software stack described in DOC-11 is likely dated. Most case data comes from Chinese plants; European cases are DOC-01 (Czech Republic), DOC-09 (UK market data) and DOC-11 (Spain).
Groups of documents that belong together
A. Furnace and hot rolling scheduling: DOC-02, DOC-07, DOC-10, DOC-15, DOC-17, with DOC-01 as a furnace case outside steel.
B. Energy use at steel plant level: DOC-05, DOC-09, DOC-12, DOC-14.
C. Steelmaking scheduling under disturbances: DOC-03, DOC-12, and DOC-02 for the rolling side.
D. Explainability, trust and the human in the loop: DOC-04, DOC-06, DOC-08, DOC-13, DOC-16.
E. Plant-wide automation architecture: DOC-11, with DOC-10 and DOC-16 on digital twins.
Group D is not about steel, but it answers a question the other groups leave open: how operators can understand and accept the schedules these algorithms produce.
3. Introduction
This report starts from a difficult position. Steel making and furnace scheduling are demanding operations in which mistakes cost energy, product quality and delivery reliability. The knowledge needed to improve them was gathered by an engineer who has since left the company, and it was left behind as a loose set of documents without an overview. Part of the reasoning behind that selection left with him.
The archive holds 17 published research papers from 2016 to 2026. Twelve deal directly with steel production, furnace scheduling or energy use. Six of them concern the scheduling of heating, soaking or reheating furnaces, and several others address plant-wide energy, electricity costs and the logistics of steelmaking. The remaining five describe supporting methods, mostly on how people can understand and trust schedules proposed by software. Most results come from Chinese plants and from simulations; one describes a prototype running at a European steel plant.
The archive does not contain internal company material. There are no memos, furnace specifications, production data or descriptions of current practice. It also says little about furnace temperature control, emissions, maintenance, standards, or how such systems are introduced on a real production floor. These gaps limit what the documents can tell us about this company directly.
The work proceeds in fixed steps. First, the basic facts of each document were extracted from the files and checked by reading. Second, every document received keywords from one shared vocabulary, so that the same subject is always named the same way. Third, the subject area was mapped: what is covered well, what thinly, and what is missing. Only after these steps does the actual analysis begin, so that later conclusions rest on a known and complete picture of the sources.
